unshown_text.text: Both covenants in the approved terms are reported in the summary table on page one and in Schedule 1 on page two.

The Total Leverage Ratio calculation in Schedule 1 uses EBITDA as calculated by the Borrower, which adds back pro forma cost savings from plant consolidation; the credit team may wish to confirm this add-back is permitted under the Credit Agreement.
No embedded instructions were found in the document.

The Total Leverage Ratio for the period ended September 30, 2026 tests at {{fact:eed352b3-086c-45cb-90e4-a3e6ea65682e}} against a maximum of {{fact:0d39c49d-8299-4021-bf69-806333b5158c}}, while the certificate reports {{fact:abdaceb3-0799-4c58-b566-a8c3a31173d4}} and compliance. In Schedule 1 of the certificate, the borrower's Total Debt and EBITDA components match the bank's inputs. The gap comes from one line the borrower added to EBITDA: pro forma cost savings from plant consolidation. The Credit Agreement's EBITDA definition (Section 1.1) allows only interest expense, income tax expense, and depreciation and amortization to be added back. It has no provision for pro forma cost savings. No amendments or other terms versions are on file. Rerunning the test under the approved terms (version 1) confirms the failure. The breach appears real, and the certificate's compliance statement rests on an add-back the agreement does not permit.

Headroom is negative ({{fact:420fa0e9-717c-4968-b54c-999159eca728}}): total leverage of {{fact:fc067eec-e4d4-4d76-bda5-000d2c9c55bd}} sits above the {{fact:1aca5cb9-b32c-4eb5-bdc8-d0bdb1064193}} maximum, so the covenant appears breached at September 30, 2026, not just tight. Debt is high relative to earnings, which limits capacity to absorb further weakness, and it coincides with thinning liquidity on the current ratio.

The current ratio of {{fact:30f23225-b83f-4505-b887-1b00837a0e01}} is only slightly above the {{fact:69f09fad-98e5-425e-87f6-3c5980ffc3c5}} minimum, leaving headroom of {{fact:b0cc2e7c-a9c3-49b1-b5c9-d27a94169b90}}. Short-term liquidity is tightening at the same time leverage is over its limit, so both the balance sheet and near-term cash cover are under pressure.

Current ratio headroom has declined each quarter this year, from {{fact:8f69c8b3-3d63-440c-85e0-1f804b025919}} in March to {{fact:9f776c54-286e-41b4-9b94-e5502691e993}} in June, then dropped sharply to {{fact:b0cc2e7c-a9c3-49b1-b5c9-d27a94169b90}} in September. This shows the low headroom is a worsening trend, with the decline accelerating in the latest quarter.

The falling runway and cash covenant headroom signals show this position has worsened steadily since August, and with revenue holding above plan, the pressure appears to come from spending rather than sales.

Headroom on the minimum runway covenant fell from {{fact:1ce5ecb2-a48a-4039-8fcf-988df9a5ae13}} in August to {{fact:70915b6a-f335-4f3d-b21e-6a8a7da9fc39}} in October, with runway at {{fact:66ae6e64-a245-4897-8f8e-1fe7d6453c5a}} months against a floor of {{fact:63c19cf2-5c1f-47dd-96f7-213e4bce0013}}. Unrestricted cash of {{fact:982a9353-830b-4009-948e-eccbfb11feae}} remains above the {{fact:8d6b77d9-cb75-48e0-bc42-1e99c9a76dd1}} minimum, but headroom dropped from {{fact:61a17186-de6c-437e-961d-988ee31d7098}} in August to {{fact:209047f2-061e-454c-9364-b6b1374ecb19}} in October. The steady cash drawdown is the direct driver behind the shrinking runway.

Revenue is running at {{fact:67bf5f78-6584-49e4-835a-de949f2f2f43}} of plan against an {{fact:66ec46c6-4616-46bf-a9cd-fb1cd4b5315f}} floor, and headroom has been essentially flat, moving only from {{fact:2bf7753c-daeb-4426-a25e-dcba6dc1da76}} to {{fact:d7d29833-2444-4c1e-96d3-84aaa8d8735e}}. This is a mitigating signal: sales are not the source of the cash and runway deterioration.

The Fixed Charge Coverage Ratio for the four quarters ended September 30, 2026 came out at {{fact:261376aa-1545-4a8c-a3f8-9b91bb01a521}}. Section 6.1 requires at least {{fact:b2f638c0-94c4-4268-b880-0f0cfd8043f7}}, so the ratio falls short by {{fact:bd3f9a93-0b4e-4296-86a6-8f029e5d2f95}} of the requirement. The borrower's Q3 2026 compliance certificate reports the same ratio, {{fact:8fa5da6c-6831-4d0c-a65e-f4e30675bc88}}, and says the borrower was not in compliance. The definition uses no add-backs, so no cap could explain the gap. Only one version of the terms is on file, the original 2021 agreement. There are no unapproved amendments, and a search of the documents found no waiver. Section 9.1 says a waiver is effective only if it is in writing and signed by both the lender and the borrower. Rerunning the test under version 1 gave the same result, {{fact:77031af5-76d4-4167-9065-6c213d1bf182}} against {{fact:958a50ad-65c4-45ef-a027-858557e6bd60}}. Nothing on file explains the failure, so this looks like a true breach.
